title: Prime Minister Razmara assassinated
summary: General Ali Razmara, the prime minister, is shot dead at a memorial service in the Shah Mosque by a member of the Fada'iyan-e Islam, a militant Islamist group. Razmara had told parliament that Iran could not run its own oil industry.
significance: His death removed the main obstacle to nationalising oil. It also showed that political Islam could be a force in Iranian politics, a generation before 1979.

title: Parliament votes to nationalise oil
summary: The Majlis votes to take over the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which had pumped Iranian oil under a British concession since 1909. The Senate follows five days later. Crowds celebrate in the streets.
significance: Iran received a small share of the profits from its own oil. Nationalisation became the great cause of Iranian nationalism, and Britain's determination to reverse it set the course for the next two years.
wiki: Nationalization of the Iranian oil industry

title: Mosaddegh becomes prime minister
summary: Mohammad Mosaddegh, an elderly aristocrat and leader of the National Front, is voted in as prime minister. Days later the Shah signs the nationalisation law, and Mosaddegh sets about carrying it out.
significance: Mosaddegh became a hero to many Iranians as the man who stood up to Britain. To London he was a fanatic who had seized a British asset.

title: British staff leave Abadan
summary: The last British oil workers sail from Abadan, home of the largest oil refinery in the world. Britain has already blockaded Iranian oil, sent warships to the Gulf and persuaded other buyers to stay away.
significance: With exports cut off, Iran lost most of its oil income. The economic squeeze weakened Mosaddegh's government over the next two years.

title: 30 Tir uprising restores Mosaddegh
summary: Mosaddegh resigns after the Shah refuses him control of the war ministry. The Shah appoints Ahmad Qavam in his place. National Front supporters, the communist Tudeh party and followers of the cleric Ayatollah Kashani pour into the streets. Troops fire on the crowds, but after a day of protest the Shah gives way and recalls Mosaddegh.
significance: A show of street power that Mosaddegh's enemies did not forget. It also left him more reliant on emergency powers and on uneasy allies.

title: First coup attempt fails; the Shah flees
summary: Late on 15 August, an officer of the Imperial Guard tries to deliver a royal decree dismissing Mosaddegh. Loyal troops arrest him. The plot, organised by the CIA and British intelligence, seems to have failed, and the Shah flies to Baghdad and then Rome.
significance: For three days Mosaddegh's supporters thought they had won. Some tore down statues of the Shah and called for a republic, which alarmed conservatives and clerics.

title: The coup: Mosaddegh overthrown
summary: Crowds, some of them paid, march from south Tehran. Army units loyal to General Fazlollah Zahedi join them, seize the radio station and shell Mosaddegh's house. By evening Mosaddegh has fled over the garden wall and Zahedi is prime minister. The Shah returns three days later.
significance: The coup was organised by the CIA (Operation Ajax) and Britain's MI6, working with royalist officers and clerics. Historians still argue about how much it owed to foreign planning and how much to Iranians who had turned against Mosaddegh. Many Iranians came to see the Shah as a ruler put back on his throne by America.

title: Oil consortium agreement
summary: Parliament approves a deal with a consortium of Western oil companies. British Petroleum keeps 40 per cent, five American companies take 40 per cent, and Shell and a French company the rest. Iran nominally owns the oil and gets half the profits.
significance: Oil flowed again and money returned to Tehran. But American companies now had a direct stake in Iran, and real control of the industry stayed in foreign hands.

title: SAVAK founded
summary: The Shah sets up SAVAK, a secret police and intelligence service, with help from American and Israeli advisers. It watches students, clerics, writers and exiles, and runs its own interrogation centres.
significance: SAVAK became the symbol of the Shah's rule. Amnesty International called Iran's human rights record among the worst in the world in the mid 1970s. The service's own officials gave lower numbers for political prisoners than its critics did, but torture of detainees is well documented.

title: The White Revolution
summary: A referendum approves the Shah's six-point reform plan: land reform, the sale of state factories, profit sharing for workers, votes for women, the nationalisation of forests, and a literacy corps. The official result is over 99 per cent in favour.
significance: The Shah meant to win over peasants and win praise from Washington. Land reform broke the power of the big landlords, but it also angered many clerics, and the votes for women and the rigged poll angered others.

title: Commandos raid the Feyziyeh seminary
summary: Security forces and plain-clothes men break up a gathering at the Feyziyeh seminary in Qom, beating students. At least one student is killed. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a senior teacher there, has been speaking out against the referendum.
significance: The raid made Khomeini the best-known opponent of the Shah among the clergy.

title: Khomeini's Ashura speech
summary: On Ashura, the day Shia Muslims mourn the martyrdom of Imam Hussein in 680, Khomeini attacks the Shah by name. He warns him not to end up like his father, who was forced out in 1941, and accuses him of serving Israel.
significance: No cleric had spoken about the Shah like this in public. Khomeini used the story of Hussein against a tyrant, a theme that returned in 1978.

title: Khomeini arrested; riots of 15 Khordad
stat: Estimates range from a few dozen to thousands killed
summary: Khomeini is arrested before dawn. Crowds riot in Tehran, Qom, Shiraz and other cities. The army, under Prime Minister Asadollah Alam, puts down the protests with live fire, and martial law is declared in Tehran.
significance: The regime called the riots reactionary. The opposition called them a massacre. After 1979 the Islamic Republic treated 15 Khordad as the start of the revolution.

title: Khomeini denounces the immunity law
summary: Parliament has granted American military personnel in Iran immunity from Iranian courts, in return for a $200 million US loan. In a speech in Qom, Khomeini calls it a surrender of Iran's independence: an Iranian who ran over an American's dog would be prosecuted, he says, but an American who ran over the Shah would not.
significance: The 'capitulation' law tied the Shah to the United States in the minds of many Iranians, and gave Khomeini a national, not only a religious, cause.

title: Khomeini exiled to Turkey
summary: Khomeini is arrested in Qom and flown into exile in Turkey. He lives under watch, mostly in Bursa, for eleven months.
significance: The Shah hoped exile would silence him. It turned him into a symbol of resistance instead.

title: Khomeini moves to Najaf
summary: Khomeini is allowed to move to Najaf in Iraq, the holy city of Shia Islam and home of its great seminaries. He will stay for thirteen years, teaching, writing and sending out statements.
significance: From Najaf, Khomeini built a network of students and supporters inside Iran. His speeches reached Iran on cassette tapes.

title: The Shah crowns himself
summary: Twenty-six years after taking the throne, Mohammad Reza Shah crowns himself and his wife Farah in the Golestan Palace. Farah is crowned Shahbanu, the first empress in modern Iranian history.
significance: The coronation marked the Shah's confidence. The 1953 crisis was long behind him, the economy was growing fast, and he presented himself as the man modernising Iran.

title: Khomeini's lectures on Islamic government
summary: In a series of lectures to his students, Khomeini argues that in the absence of the hidden Imam, Muslims should be ruled by a just and learned Islamic jurist. The lectures are published as a book, Islamic Government.
significance: This idea, velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist), became the basis of the Islamic Republic's constitution in 1979. Many senior clerics rejected it at the time.

title: Guerrillas attack at Siahkal
summary: A small band of Marxist guerrillas attacks a gendarmerie post in the forests of Gilan, near the Caspian. The army hunts them down within weeks, and thirteen are later executed.
significance: Militarily a failure, Siahkal launched the Fadai guerrillas. With the Islamic-leftist Mojahedin, they waged a campaign of bombings and shootings through the 1970s. Both groups later played a part in the fighting of February 1979.

title: 2,500 years of monarchy at Persepolis
summary: The Shah hosts kings, presidents and princes in a city of luxury tents beside the ruins of Persepolis, to celebrate 2,500 years since Cyrus the Great. Food and wine are flown in from Paris. Two days later he opens the Shahyad Tower in Tehran.
significance: The Shah meant to link his dynasty to ancient Persia. Critics pointed to the cost, which estimates put from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, at a time of rural poverty. From Najaf, Khomeini condemned it as a festival of tyrants.

title: Oil price quadruples
summary: At a meeting in Tehran, Gulf oil producers set the posted price of crude at $11.65 a barrel, more than double the October price and about four times the price at the start of the year. The Shah announces the decision himself.
significance: Iran's oil income soared, from about $555 million in 1963 to about $20 billion by 1975. The Shah doubled his spending plans overnight.

title: One-party state: the Rastakhiz party
summary: The Shah abolishes Iran's two official parties and creates one, Rastakhiz (Resurgence). Iranians who will not join, he says, can leave the country. Later that year the party sends students to hunt 'profiteers' in the bazaars, and thousands of shopkeepers are fined or jailed.
significance: The oil boom brought high inflation, housing shortages and migration to the cities. Blaming the bazaar for prices drove the merchants, long tied to the clergy, into opposition.

title: Ten nights of poetry
summary: The Iranian Writers' Association holds ten nights of readings in the garden of the German cultural institute. Thousands come to hear poets and writers speak openly about censorship.
significance: Under pressure from US President Carter over human rights, the Shah had loosened control a little. Liberal and secular critics were first to test the new space.

title: Carter: 'an island of stability'
summary: On a New Year's Eve visit, President Jimmy Carter toasts the Shah, calling Iran 'an island of stability' in a troubled region.
significance: Within thirteen months the Shah would be gone. The toast became a byword for how badly Washington misread Iran.

title: Newspaper attack on Khomeini
summary: The newspaper Ettela'at prints an article, written under a false name and approved by the court, that smears Khomeini as a foreign agent. It comes weeks after his son Mostafa died suddenly in Najaf, a death many Iranians blamed on SAVAK.
significance: The article was meant to discredit Khomeini. It set off the protest that began the revolution.
wiki: Iran and Red and Black Colonization

title: Police fire on seminary students in Qom
stat: Reports range from a few dead to over 70
summary: Seminary students and their supporters march in Qom against the article. Police open fire.
significance: In Shia custom the dead are mourned on the fortieth day. Each mourning ceremony now turned into a new protest, which brought new deaths, and so a new mourning forty days later. This cycle drove the revolution through 1978.

title: Tabriz rises on the fortieth day
stat: Officially about a dozen dead; the opposition said hundreds
summary: Forty days after Qom, mourners in Tabriz find a mosque locked by police. The crowd riots, attacking banks, cinemas, liquor shops and Rastakhiz offices. The army is called in to restore order.
significance: The first time the army was used against crowds in the revolution. The government blamed 'Islamic Marxists' and outside agitators.

title: Mourning protests spread; deaths in Yazd
summary: Forty days after Tabriz, mourning ceremonies are held in dozens of cities. In Yazd, police fire on a crowd leaving a mosque, and several people are killed. Another forty days later, in May, protests break out again.
significance: The protests were now national. The Shah alternated between concessions and force, which emboldened some and enraged others.

title: Cinema Rex fire
summary: Arsonists set fire to the Cinema Rex in Abadan during an evening showing. The doors are locked or blocked, and hundreds of people burn to death.
significance: At the time most Iranians believed SAVAK had set the fire to discredit the religious opposition, and the disaster turned many against the Shah. After the revolution, a court found that an Islamist militant, Hossein Takbalizadeh, and his accomplices had started it. He was executed in 1980. Who ordered the fire, if anyone, is still disputed.

title: Eid al-Fitr march
summary: At the end of Ramadan, a huge crowd prays in the open at Qeytarieh in north Tehran and then marches peacefully across the city to Shahyad Square. A new prime minister, Jafar Sharif-Emami, has promised 'national reconciliation': he has closed casinos and restored the Islamic calendar. The crowds want more.
significance: Tehran's middle classes joined the clergy and the bazaar on the streets. Three days later a still larger march called for the Shah's fall.

title: Black Friday at Jaleh Square
stat: Government: 86 dead across Tehran. Opposition at the time: thousands. A later count by the Martyrs Foundation: 64 at Jaleh Square, 88 in Tehran that day
summary: Martial law is declared in Tehran and eleven other cities overnight. Next morning thousands gather in Jaleh Square, many unaware of the ban. Troops order them to leave, then open fire.
significance: Black Friday ended hopes of compromise. Whatever the real toll, the belief that thousands had died put a sea of blood between the Shah and the people. The square was renamed Shohada, the Square of the Martyrs.

title: Khomeini moves to Paris
summary: Under pressure from Tehran, Iraq forces Khomeini to leave Najaf. Kuwait turns him away at the border, so he flies to Paris and settles in a village outside the city.
significance: The move backfired on the Shah. In France Khomeini gave hundreds of interviews to the world's press, and his statements reached Iran by phone and cassette within hours.

title: Oil workers strike
summary: Oil workers in Khuzestan join a wave of strikes by civil servants, bank staff and factory workers. They demand an end to martial law, the release of political prisoners and higher pay. Output collapses, and by late December Iran is exporting almost no oil.
significance: The strikes starved the government of money and fuel. Without oil the regime could not outlast the protests.

title: Troops fire on students at the university
summary: Students pull down a statue of the Shah at the University of Tehran. Soldiers open fire, killing several. Film of the shooting is shown on state television.
significance: The killings set off the worst riots yet the next day.

title: Tehran burns; the Shah 'hears the revolution'
summary: Crowds set fire to banks, cinemas, liquor stores and part of the British embassy while troops largely stand aside. The next day the Shah appoints a military government under General Gholam-Reza Azhari. On television he tells the nation: 'I have heard the voice of your revolution.'
significance: The Shah mixed apology and force, and neither worked. He was also secretly ill with cancer, which few people knew.

title: Tasu'a march
stat: Estimates for Tehran range from a few hundred thousand to over a million
summary: On the eve of Ashura, a vast and orderly crowd marches across Tehran to Shahyad Square. The government has lifted the ban on marches after the organisers promise to keep the peace. The march is led by Ayatollah Taleghani and the National Front leader Karim Sanjabi.
significance: The clergy, the bazaar, the secular National Front and the left marched together. It was the largest protest in Iran's history to that point.

title: Ashura march to Shahyad Square
stat: Estimates for Tehran range from a few hundred thousand to two million
summary: On the day of Ashura an even bigger crowd marches along Shahreza and Eisenhower Avenues to Shahyad Square. There a seventeen-point resolution is read out. It names Khomeini leader, calls for the end of the monarchy and demands social justice.
significance: The marches were a referendum on the street. Foreign diplomats reported that the Shah could no longer rule.

title: The Shah leaves Iran
summary: The Shah and Farah fly out of Mehrabad, officially for a holiday. He leaves power with Shapour Bakhtiar, a National Front veteran who has just become prime minister. Crowds pour into the streets, cheering and honking horns. Newspapers print the headline 'The Shah is gone.'
significance: Bakhtiar freed political prisoners, dissolved SAVAK and promised free elections. But his old allies expelled him from the National Front, and Khomeini called his government illegal.

title: Khomeini returns
summary: After nearly fifteen years in exile, Khomeini lands at Mehrabad on a chartered Air France jet. Huge crowds line the route. At the Behesht-e Zahra cemetery, among the graves of those killed in the protests, he declares Bakhtiar's government illegal: 'I will appoint a government.'
significance: Asked on the plane what he felt about returning, Khomeini answered, 'Nothing.' The remark became famous, read either as spiritual detachment or as a warning.

title: Bazargan named head of a provisional government
summary: From his headquarters at the Alavi School, Khomeini names Mehdi Bazargan, a devout engineer and liberal, as prime minister of a provisional government. Iran now has two governments.
significance: Bazargan stood for a moderate, legal revolution. His government would be overshadowed from the start by the revolutionary committees and courts loyal to Khomeini.

title: Air force cadets mutiny
summary: Air force technicians, the homafaran, cheer Khomeini at their base. The Imperial Guard attacks them, and they fight back. Fadai and Mojahedin guerrillas and armed civilians join in, and weapons are handed out to the crowds.
significance: The fighting spread across Tehran over two days. The last loyal units of the army now faced an armed city.

title: The army stands aside: the revolution wins
summary: Police stations, barracks and the radio station fall to revolutionaries. The armed forces' Supreme Council declares itself neutral. Bakhtiar goes into hiding and later escapes to France. State radio announces: 'This is the voice of Tehran, the voice of true Iran, the voice of the revolution.'
significance: 2,500 years of monarchy were over. Iranians mark 22 Bahman as the anniversary of the revolution.

title: First executions on the school roof
summary: After secret trials by a revolutionary court, four of the Shah's generals are shot on the roof of the Refah School, where Khomeini is staying. They include Nematollah Nassiri, a former head of SAVAK.
significance: Hundreds more executions of officials, officers and alleged counter-revolutionaries followed in 1979. Bazargan's government protested at the speed of the trials but could not stop them.

title: Women march against compulsory veiling
summary: On International Women's Day, after Khomeini says women in government offices should wear the hijab, tens of thousands of women march in Tehran. Protests continue for several days.
significance: The government stepped back for a while. Compulsory veiling was imposed in stages from 1980 and became law in 1983.
wiki: 1979 International Women's Day protests in Tehran

title: Fighting in Kurdistan
summary: Fighting breaks out in Sanandaj between Kurdish groups and revolutionary forces. Kurdish parties, led by the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran, demand self-rule within Iran and take control of much of the region.
significance: Kurds, Turkmen, Arabs and Baluch all pressed for rights in the new Iran. Tehran saw separatism and foreign plots, and answered with force.

title: Iran votes for an Islamic Republic
summary: In a referendum on 30 and 31 March, voters are asked one question: should Iran be an Islamic Republic, yes or no? Khomeini, now living in Qom, declares the Islamic Republic on 1 April.
significance: Liberals and the left had asked for more choices on the ballot. Some groups, including the National Democratic Front and some Kurdish parties, boycotted the vote.

title: Ayatollah Motahhari assassinated
summary: Morteza Motahhari, a leading cleric and one of Khomeini's closest students, is shot dead by Forqan, a small group that opposed clerical rule.
significance: One of several killings of revolutionary leaders in 1979 and after. The new state used them to justify harsher measures against its opponents.

title: Khomeini orders the army into Kurdistan
summary: Kurdish fighters besiege Revolutionary Guards in the town of Paveh. Khomeini, as commander-in-chief, orders the army and the Guards to crush the revolt. Kurdish towns are retaken over the following weeks, and revolutionary courts execute dozens of Kurds.
significance: Fighting in Kurdistan went on for years. The Kurdish question was one of the first tests of the new republic's power.

title: Students seize the US embassy
stat: 66 Americans taken hostage; 52 held for 444 days
summary: Students calling themselves the Muslim Student Followers of the Imam's Line climb the walls of the US embassy and take its staff hostage. They demand that America hand over the Shah, who was admitted to New York for cancer treatment in October. Khomeini backs them.
significance: Supporters saw it as revenge for 1953 and a blow against a 'den of spies'. In the US and much of the world it was a breach of diplomatic law. Inside Iran, the crisis helped hardliners push aside moderates.

title: Bazargan resigns
summary: Unable to free the hostages or control the revolutionary bodies, Mehdi Bazargan and his cabinet resign. The Revolutionary Council, dominated by clerics, takes over.
significance: The end of the moderate, liberal wing of the revolution's leadership.

title: New constitution approved
stat: Official result: over 99 per cent yes
summary: A referendum on 2 and 3 December approves the new constitution. It gives supreme authority to a leading Islamic jurist, the Faqih, with Khomeini in the post for life. It also creates an elected president and parliament.
significance: Velayat-e faqih was now law. Ayatollah Shariatmadari, the most senior cleric in Iran, objected to it, and his followers in Tabriz rose in protest days later.
wiki: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran

title: Banisadr elected president
stat: About 76 per cent of the vote
summary: Abolhassan Banisadr, an economist close to Khomeini in Paris, wins the first presidential election by a landslide.
significance: Banisadr soon clashed with the clerics of the Islamic Republican Party. He was impeached in June 1981 and fled to France.

title: Operation Eagle Claw fails
summary: A US rescue mission lands at a desert strip codenamed Desert One. Three of eight helicopters break down, and the mission is aborted. As the force leaves, a helicopter collides with a transport plane. Eight American servicemen die.
significance: The failure humiliated the Carter administration. The hostages were scattered to different places to stop another attempt. Khomeini's supporters said God had sent the sandstorms.

title: The universities close
summary: Supporters of the Islamic Republican Party storm campuses to drive out leftist student groups, and people are killed in the clashes. The universities are shut for what is called a Cultural Revolution, to purge them of Western and leftist influence.
significance: The universities stayed closed until 1983. Thousands of lecturers and students were purged.

title: The Shah dies in exile
summary: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi dies of cancer in Cairo, aged 60, after moving between Egypt, Morocco, the Bahamas, Mexico, the United States and Panama. President Sadat gives him a state funeral.
significance: His death removed the hostage-takers' main demand, though the crisis went on for six more months.

title: Saddam tears up the border treaty
summary: Iraq's president Saddam Hussein cancels the 1975 Algiers Agreement, which had set the border along the middle of the Shatt al-Arab river. Iraq claims the whole waterway.
significance: Saddam saw Iran's army purged and in chaos, and feared Khomeini's calls to Iraq's Shia majority to rise up. He expected a short war.

title: Iraq invades Iran
summary: Iraqi jets bomb Iranian airfields, including Mehrabad. Iraqi divisions cross the border on a wide front, with the main thrust into oil-rich Khuzestan, whose people are largely Arab.
significance: The invasion rallied Iranians around the new regime. The war lasted eight years and killed hundreds of thousands.

title: Khorramshahr falls
summary: After a month of house-to-house fighting, Iraqi forces take the port of Khorramshahr. Revolutionary Guards and local volunteers had held them far longer than expected. Iranians call it Khuninshahr, the city of blood.
significance: Abadan, across the river, was besieged but never taken. Iran retook Khorramshahr in May 1982.

title: Hostages released after 444 days
summary: Under the Algiers Accords, the US unfreezes billions of dollars of Iranian assets and Iran releases the 52 remaining hostages. Their plane leaves Mehrabad minutes after Ronald Reagan is sworn in as president.
significance: The crisis cost Carter re-election and set Iran and America on a course of hostility that has lasted ever since.
